teaching.task: # HMS Year 12 V02 (Training for improved performance): fitness testing and exercise assessment. What makes a fitness test worth running, and how does its result actually shape a training program? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: In Year 11 you met two checks on any measurement: validity, whether it measures what it claims to, and reliability, whether it gives the same result again when the athlete hasn't changed. Testing adds two more. Specificity: does the test match this sport's demands? Timing a rower over a forty-metre sprint fails that. Objectivity: would two testers score it the same? A coach judging technique by eye fails that. A vertical jump is a valid test of leg power, and an invalid test of endurance, however carefully you run it. Reliability is bought with protocol, the fixed conditions, equipment and scoring rules. Same surface, shoes, time of day, warm-up and scorer. Each one you hold constant removes a rival explanation. That's why an unreliable test is worse than no test. It produces a number that looks like evidence. Testing starts from a question, not a test. Which quality is limiting this athlete right now? Name it, and the test follows. Aerobic capacity, a shuttle run. Strength, a one-rep max, the heaviest load lifted once. Power, a vertical jump. Speed, a timed sprint. The syllabus names two tests for a reason. The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test isn't a continuous run. Shuttles alternate with short active rests, so it measures what team-sport players need: repeated efforts with incomplete recovery. The Wingate test is a thirty-second, all-out anaerobic sprint on a bike against a fixed resistance. It reports peak power, mean power, and how far power drops by the end. Say a cyclist peaks at a thousand watts and finishes at six hundred. The drop is four hundred, divided by a thousand, so a forty per cent fatigue index.

scenes.teachingReason: In Year 11 you met two checks on any measurement: validity, whether it measures what it claims to, and reliability, whether it gives the same result again when the athlete hasn't changed. Testing adds two more. Specificity: does the test match this sport's demands? Timing a rower over a forty-metre sprint fails that. Objectivity: would two testers score it the same? A coach judging technique by eye fails that. A vertical jump is a valid test of leg power, and an invalid test of endurance, however carefully you run it. Reliability is bought with protocol, the fixed conditions, equipment and scoring rules. Same surface, shoes, time of day, warm-up and scorer. Each one you hold constant removes a rival explanation. That's why an unreliable test is worse than no test. It produces a number that looks like evidence.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus names two tests for a reason. The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test isn't a continuous run. Shuttles alternate with short active rests, so it measures what team-sport players need: repeated efforts with incomplete recovery. The Wingate test is a thirty-second, all-out anaerobic sprint on a bike against a fixed resistance. It reports peak power, mean power, and how far power drops by the end. Say a cyclist peaks at a thousand watts and finishes at six hundred. The drop is four hundred, divided by a thousand, so a forty per cent fatigue index.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus names two groups, and they want different things from testing. For a recreational participant, testing is about health, motivation and a safe starting point. The measures are simple: resting heart rate, blood pressure, waist size, and a submaximal aerobic estimate, where the person never works flat out. It only needs to catch a meaningful health change, every few months. For an elite athlete, testing diagnoses performance and informs selection. The measures are sport-specific, precise enough that the test's own error is smaller than the small changes that matter at the top level, and repeated through the season. And the risks differ. A maximal test can put a beginner off exercise, while for an elite athlete the cost is lost training time. So recreational testing supports health and participation, and elite testing earns its place only if it changes a decision.

scenes.teachingReason: Now, how assessment builds the program. It does four separate jobs. First, it sets the baseline, the first measurement that every later one is compared with. Intensity is set as a share of something measured, like the maximum heart rate from Year 11, or a one-rep max. Without a baseline, it's a guess. Second, it finds the limiter, the component holding performance back. Third, it makes the goal specific, a target score on a test the athlete has already done. Fourth, it closes the loop. Re-testing with the same protocol is the only evidence the block worked. A seventeen-year-old club netballer has a strong Yo-Yo score, an average vertical jump, and a big difference between legs on a single-leg hop. So the block puts lower-body power first, adds single-leg work, keeps aerobic work at maintenance, and re-tests both jumps, on the same surface, in the same shoes.

scenes.teachingReason: A result has four limits. Motivation is part of the score: trying harder the second time raises it with no change in fitness. Protocol drifts. Surface, shoes, heat, time of day, and who's counting all move a score. Ecological validity, how well a test copies the real sport, is limited. A bike in a lab has no tackles, decisions or changes of direction. And a test measures a component, not an athlete. Now back to the coach's beep test. Four rival explanations compete with the training. The fix isn't to stop testing. Standardise the protocol, judge change against normal variation, and read the results beside what the coach sees in games.

scenes.motionPurpose:
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".

1. A defensible test: valid, reliable, specific, objective; protocol buys reliability.
2. Choose from the limiter. Yo-Yo: repeated effort, incomplete recovery.
3. Wingate: 30 s all-out; peak power, mean power, fatigue index (% drop).
4. Recreational: health, motivation, submax. Elite: precise, changes a decision.
5. Assessment: baseline, limiter, target, re-test (same protocol).

Memory card (the scene 7 card) beside the notes. Each bullet one line of at most 86 characters. Hold about 45 seconds in all.
